title: Sales & Distribution Management (MBA)
source: SDM course decks (Intro, Sessions 2, 3, 4–5, 6) and handwritten class notes
purpose: Revising for an MBA Sales & Distribution Management exam.
about: Frameworks, definitions, processes in order and two short numericals. Refs point to the parts of the consolidated exam notes and the source slides.

sections.title: Sales management basics
sections.why: The definition and the selling-vs-marketing contrast turn up in almost every paper.

questions.prompt: Define sales management.
questions.answer: The **planning, organising, leading and controlling** of personal contact programmes designed to achieve the **sales and profit** objectives of the firm.

mcq.prompt: Sales management is planning, organising, leading and controlling personal contact programmes to achieve…
options: The firm's sales and profit objectives
mcq.why: Sales **and profit**. Modern sales management is profit-oriented, not volume-oriented.

questions.prompt: Under the marketing concept, how are price and cost related?
options: The consumer sets the price, and price determines cost
Price is fixed by the sales team's targets
Cost and price are set independently
questions.answer: Selling concept: **cost determines price**. Marketing concept: **consumers determine price, and price determines cost**.

questions.prompt: Which belong to the **selling** orientation rather than marketing? Pick all that apply.
options: Customer seen as the last link in the business
Innovation in every sphere to give better value
questions.answer: Selling: volume, short run, seller's needs, customer as last link, water-tight departments. Marketing: profit, long run, buyer's needs, customer as the purpose, integrated departments, innovation.

questions.prompt: Which shift is one of the slide's sales management trends?
options: From sales volume to sales productivity
questions.answer: The five trends: transactions → relationships, individuals → teams, **volume → productivity**, management → leadership, local → global.

questions.prompt: Which skill does the deck say matters most for today's sales manager?
questions.answer: “People skills” are more important than analytical and evaluative skills. The modern manager coaches and communicates more than they monitor and control.

questions.prompt: A sales manager's DSO keeps rising. What does it signal?
questions.hint: DSO counts days of sales not yet collected.
options: More working capital is tied up in unpaid customer bills
Sales calls per day are falling
The sales forecast is too optimistic
questions.answer: **DSO (days sales outstanding)** measures how long customers take to pay. Higher DSO means more money stuck in receivables, so working capital needs go up. It is a sales-manager KRA alongside forecast accuracy, skewness, revenue and margin.

questions.prompt: Order these from the goal to the action.
questions.hint: What you want, how you'll get it, what people do.
questions.answer: **Objectives** (specific, measurable goals) → **strategies** (plans of action) → **tactics** (the activities people perform to carry out the strategy).

sections.title: How buyers buy
sections.why: Selling starts with knowing who decides and how.

questions.prompt: Put the consumer buying decision process in order.
questions.answer: Need arousal → information → evaluation → purchase → post-purchase feelings: **satisfaction** or **cognitive dissonance**.

questions.prompt: Put the business buying process in order.
questions.hint: Specify before you search; review comes last.
questions.answer: Eight stages. **Proposal solicitation** invites qualified suppliers to bid; **order-routine specification** writes the final order (specs, quantity, delivery, returns, warranty, payment terms).

questions.prompt: Which are buying-centre roles on the slide? Pick all that apply.
questions.hint: Who uses, who sways, who signs, who places the order, who controls access.
questions.answer: Five on the slide: **users, influencers, deciders, buyers, gatekeepers**. Kotler adds initiators and approvers. Distributors are channel members, not buying-centre roles.

questions.prompt: A firm reorders the same office paper from the same supplier. What buying situation is this?
questions.answer: **Straight rebuy**: routine, low priority. **Modified rebuy**: some specs, prices or suppliers change. **New task**: first-time, judgmental, strategic. (Extensive decision making is a consumer decision type.)

questions.prompt: Which is a buyer's **personal** goal rather than an organisational one?
questions.hint: Something the buyer wants for themselves.
questions.answer: Personal goals: power, pleasure, **job security**, being liked, respect. Organisational: cost control, reliability, dependable delivery, adequate supply, budget. A good pitch serves both.

sections.title: The art of selling
sections.why: The selling process and its acronyms are standard 5- and 10-mark questions.

questions.prompt: Put the personal selling process in order.
questions.hint: Find them, research them, meet them, understand them…
questions.answer: Prospecting → pre-approach → approach → need assessment → presentation → objections → close → follow-up.

questions.prompt: Which step of the selling process is the only one that produces revenue?
questions.answer: **Closing** is the only revenue-producing step, and the hardest, because of the salesperson's fear of rejection. Keep it simple, honest and direct.

questions.prompt: In need assessment, what does LOCATE stand for?
questions.hint: Starts with Listen, ends with Empathise.
options: Listen, Observe, Combine, Ask questions, Talk to others, Empathise
Learn, Offer, Close, Ask, Track, Evaluate
Listen, Organise, Clarify, Act, Test, Explain
Locate, Observe, Contact, Approach, Talk, Engage
questions.answer: **L**isten, **O**bserve, **C**ombine, **A**sk questions, **T**alk to others, **E**mpathise: ways to uncover needs the prospect may not state.

questions.prompt: In the SELL sequence, what does the first L ask the salesperson to do?
questions.answer: **S**how the feature → **E**xplain the advantage → **L**ead into the benefit → **L**et the customer talk (ask an opinion question). It's the FAB logic.

questions.prompt: John Salley had top grades and deep product knowledge, yet only average sales. What was going wrong?
questions.hint: He knew the product. Did he know the customer?

keyPoints.text: Should listen and use need assessment

questions.answer: He talked **features** the customer didn't need. The fix: uncover needs (LOCATE), translate features into **benefits** (SELL/FAB), listen more, and work on the psychology of selling.

mcq.prompt: Why were John Salley's sales only average?
options: He sold product features instead of uncovering needs and selling benefits
His territory had too little potential
mcq.why: Knowledge wasn't the gap. Customers buy solutions, so he needed to find needs and sell benefits.

questions.prompt: What is the “hot button”?
options: The buyer's most highly emotional reason for buying
The final price the buyer will accept
questions.answer: People buy for rational and emotional reasons. The **hot button** is the most highly emotional one (for example respect or status).

questions.prompt: Self-concept has three parts. Which? Pick all that apply.
questions.hint: How you see yourself, who you want to be, how you feel about yourself.
questions.answer: **Self-image** (how you see yourself), **self-ideal** (how you'd like to be), **self-esteem** (how much you like yourself).

questions.prompt: Which selling approach focuses on the customer's strategic objectives?
questions.answer: Stimulus–response and mental states (AIDA) suit simple transactions. Need satisfaction and problem solving suit solutions. **Consultative** selling serves partnerships and collaboration.

questions.prompt: Moving from transactional to partnership relationships, what happens to cost to serve?
questions.hint: Look at the class graph's axes.
options: It rises, along with commitment to the customer
questions.answer: Transactional → relationship → partnership: **commitment** and **cost to serve** both rise. Only accounts worth it should get partnerships.

sections.title: Potential, forecasts and quotas
sections.why: The potential-vs-forecast distinction and forecasting methods are classic exam material.

questions.prompt: Market potential is measured for…
options: The whole industry in a market and period
One firm's expected sales under its plan
questions.answer: **Market potential**: total expected industry sales. **Sales potential**: a firm's maximum reasonable share. **Sales forecast**: what the firm expects under its marketing plan.

questions.prompt: Order from largest to smallest, as they usually stand.
questions.hint: Industry ceiling, firm ceiling, firm's realistic plan.
questions.answer: Market potential ≥ sales potential ≥ sales forecast. The forecast sits below sales potential because of capacity and financial limits.

questions.prompt: When are market potential and sales potential equal?
questions.answer: With a **monopoly**, the firm *is* the industry, so its sales potential equals market potential.

questions.prompt: Why is a sales forecast usually below sales potential? Pick all that apply.
options: Limited finance (working capital, cash, ad budget)
Competitors take part of the market
The forecast ignores the marketing plan
questions.answer: Internal limits: **capacity** (plant, warehouse) and **finance**. Competition explains the gap between *market* and *sales* potential, not this one. The forecast is always tied to a proposed marketing plan.

questions.prompt: Which method of estimating potential is probably the most accurate?
questions.answer: **Test markets**: buyers spend real money, the acid test. But they're slow, costly, and impossible for products needing big fixed investment before launch.

questions.prompt: What is a market factor?
options: Something that causes demand or is related to it
questions.answer: A **market factor** causes demand or moves with it. Market factor derivation is valid, simple, needs little statistics and is cheap.

questions.prompt: The sales force composite method is…
options: Bottom-up: each rep estimates their own territory
Statistical: based on past sales only
Experimental: based on a test market
questions.answer: **Bottom-up**. Reps are close to customers, but may lowball forecasts to get easier quotas.

questions.prompt: Last forecast 110, last actual 120, α = 0.3. What is the exponential-smoothing forecast?
questions.answer: F = 110 + 0.3 × (120 − 110) = **113**. Exponential smoothing weights recent sales more; higher α reacts faster.

mcq.prompt: Which formula gives the exponential-smoothing forecast?
mcq.why: Old forecast plus α times the last error. The second option is a moving average.

questions.prompt: A moving average forecast works best for products with…
questions.hint: It treats all recent periods equally.
questions.answer: Moving average = sum of the last n periods ÷ n. Good for **stable** patterns; it lags turns because old and new data weigh the same.

questions.prompt: Which budgeting method costs the tasks needed to hit the objectives?
questions.answer: **Objective and task**: set objectives, cost the tasks. **Percentage of sales**: simple, but treats sales as the cause of spending.

questions.prompt: Which are purposes of sales quotas? Pick all that apply.
options: Indicate strong and weak spots in the selling structure
questions.answer: Quotas indicate strong/weak spots, give goals and incentives, control activities, evaluate productivity, improve compensation plans and control expenses. They don't set prices.

questions.prompt: Which is a feature of a good quota plan?
questions.hint: Can the rep actually hit it?
options: Set as high as possible to stretch reps
Kept vague so managers can adjust it
questions.answer: Good quotas are **realistic, objective, easy to understand, flexible and fair**.

sections.title: Territories and deployment
sections.why: Territory design and the workload calculation are the main numerical in the course.

questions.prompt: The build-up method of territory design equalises…
questions.hint: Build up from the calls needed.
questions.answer: **Build-up** = equal **workload** (accounts × call frequency). **Break-down** = equal **sales potential**.

questions.prompt: Territory Y: 5 A-accounts at 24 calls a year, 15 B at 12, 60 C at 6. Total calls a year?
questions.answer: 5×24 + 15×12 + 60×6 = 120 + 180 + 360 = **660**. Territory X in class was 540, so Y is overloaded.

mcq.prompt: How do you calculate a territory's workload?
options: Sum of (accounts in each class × call frequency for that class)
Number of accounts × number of salespeople
Total calls ÷ calls one rep can make
mcq.why: Workload = Σ accounts × calls. Dividing total calls by one rep's capacity gives the number of reps needed, the next step.

questions.prompt: Put the territory design steps in order.
questions.hint: Smallest unit first, assign people last.
questions.answer: Control unit → criteria → starting point → combine → workload analysis → modify → assign.

questions.prompt: An account has high potential, and you're in a strong position. What's the strategy?
questions.answer: Account opportunity grid: high potential + strong = **commit heavily**. Low + strong = maintain. High + weak = invest to improve or shift. Low + weak = minimal or abandon.

questions.prompt: Put the sales force deployment stages in order.
questions.answer: **Audit** goals, strategy, constraints, resources, data → **assess** potential and workload → **prescribe** alignment → **monitor**.

questions.prompt: When should territories be aligned on market potential rather than workload?
options: When equitable earning opportunity matters most
When account coverage is the key success factor
questions.answer: Balance **workload** when coverage is critical. Balance **potential** when fair pay opportunity is needed to attract and motivate reps.

questions.prompt: In the pricing waterfall, what sits between invoice price and pocket price?
questions.hint: Money that leaks after the invoice.
options: Off-invoice leakages like rebates, credit costs and returns
questions.answer: List price → on-invoice discounts → **invoice price** → off-invoice leakages → **pocket price** → minus COGS and cost-to-serve → **pocket margin**.

sections.title: Building the sales team
sections.why: Assessment centres, training evaluation and motivation are favourite theory questions.

questions.prompt: Put the staffing process in order.
questions.hint: Plan, find, pick, offer, settle in.
questions.answer: Planning → recruitment → selection → hiring → **assimilation** (joining, policies, culture, socialisation).

questions.prompt: Which would **not** count as an assessment centre? Pick all that apply.
questions.hint: ACs need many observers, many exercises, pooled data.
options: Only a battery of paper-and-pencil tests
A panel interview as the only technique
Several simulations with several assessors and pooled data
questions.answer: Not ACs: single assessor, only written tests, interviews alone, a single technique, or no pooling of data. A real AC uses multiple trained observers, exercises and pooled judgments.

questions.prompt: What does the deck call the most critical aspect of an assessment centre?
questions.answer: **Observation** is the most critical element, which is why ACs use multiple trained observers and test each competency in at least two exercises.

questions.prompt: Which are uses of assessment centres? Pick all that apply.
questions.answer: Selection, career development, potential appraisal, high-potential identification, succession planning, challenging assignments, management development, training needs, global talent pools.

questions.prompt: Put Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation in order.
questions.hint: From how they felt to what changed in the business.
questions.answer: **Reactions** (feedback) → **learning** (tested) → **behaviour** (on the job) → **results** (performance).

questions.prompt: “I'm concerned about your call ratios. You've always been a top performer. What's up?” Which quadrant?
questions.answer: Coaching uses facts and logic; counselling uses emotion and empathy. A warm, emotional opener is **positive counselling**.

questions.prompt: What are the three dimensions of motivation? Pick all that apply.
questions.hint: Which way, how hard, how long.
questions.answer: **Direction** (choice of action), **intensity** (effort), **persistence** (how long). Compensation is a motivator, not a dimension.

questions.prompt: A rep asks, “If I try harder, will my numbers actually go up?” Which link is this?
questions.answer: **Expectancy**: effort → performance. **Instrumentality**: performance → reward. **Valence**: is the reward worth it? Weak links kill motivation.

questions.prompt: Order a salesperson's career stages.
questions.answer: Each stage needs different motivators: coaching early, promotion when establishing, recognition and fresh challenges in maintenance, security near disengagement.

questions.prompt: In a commission plan, what is the “base”?
options: The point from which commission starts being paid
questions.answer: **Base** = where commission starts; **rate** = the % or amount paid above it. Method of pay: fixed, variable, or combination.

sections.title: Channels and intermediaries
sections.why: Why channels exist, and what flows through them, anchors the distribution half.

questions.prompt: What is a marketing channel?
options: A set of interdependent organisations that make a product available for use or consumption
questions.answer: A **marketing channel** is a set of interdependent organisations involved in making a product or service available for use or consumption. Sales plans; distribution executes.

questions.prompt: Which gaps justify intermediaries? Pick all that apply.
questions.answer: **Temporal** (time), **spatial** (place), **bulk** (lot size) and **assortment** (variety). Intermediaries close them.

questions.prompt: Put the sorting functions in order.
questions.answer: Sort out mixed supply → **accumulate** homogeneous stock → **allocate** into smaller lots → **assort** a range for buyers.

questions.prompt: 5 manufacturers each sell to 10 customers. How many contacts are saved by routing everything through one intermediary?
questions.hint: Direct = M × C. Via one = M + C.
questions.answer: Direct: 5 × 10 = 50. Via one intermediary: 5 + 10 = 15. **35 fewer** contacts.

mcq.prompt: How many contacts are needed with one intermediary between M makers and C customers?
mcq.why: Each party deals only with the intermediary. Direct dealing needs M × C.

questions.prompt: Which channel flow moves backward, from customer towards manufacturer?
questions.answer: Forward: possession, ownership, promotion. **Backward: ordering, payment.** Both ways: negotiation, financing, risk, information.

questions.prompt: Manufacturer → C&FA → Distributor → Retailer is how many tiers?
questions.answer: C&FA, distributor, retailer: **3-tier**, common in Indian FMCG. A C&FA holds regional stock for the maker, usually without owning it.
